items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: Shelly Manne and Steve Gadd are the new guys... It’s sort of like groovin’ what they did in the band

ctx.x: You’ve got it covered. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -14-

But you know it’s great fun when you’re doing something that you really love to do, it’s a lot of fun, and as long as I can keep doing it I’ll be hitting rim shots and crashing cymbals. Oh yeah, I got a new CD now that was just released on Concord, and I’ve always wanted to do this, it’s a salute honoring twelve great drummers, most of them from the back era and some are in the present state, and a few that are still living, like starting with Chick Webb, Big Sid Catlett, Jo Jones, Buddy, Gene, Elvin Jones, Tony…
Oh, boy, that’s quite a project, to try to capture all the —

items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I’d call Shelly Manne or Earl Palmer or Paul Humphrey. We’d always look out for one another. Drummers were very close, and we would go hear one another

ctx.x: It sounds like the drummers was a fraternity of sorts. It sounds like you guys had a real rapport and looked out for one another? Is that really the case?

Oh yeah, yes, absolutely. To the extent, if one guy couldn’t make – like if I was out in California working for Quincy Jones and I couldn’t make a certain date, I’d call Shelly Manne or Earl Palmer or Paul Humphrey. We’d always look out for one another. Drummers were very close, and we would go hear one another, like Buddy Rich coming to hear me play. I’d go hear him play. One thing about him: he always used to cop my hi- hat and my snare drum. I’d come to the gig at night, and no snare drum and hi-hat. Good…
When’s the first time you met Buddy Rich? Do you remember meeting him for the first time?
